data:
Numerical integration and ODE solvers in pure Go (CGO_ENABLED=0): adaptive quadrature (QUADPACK), fixed and sample rules, multiple integrals, and initial value problems with RK45, RK23, DOP853, Radau, BDF and automatic stiffness switching — the functionality of scipy.integrate for the Go scientific stack (go-ndarray, go-plot, go-notebook), with the same algorithms, defaults and diagnostics.
go get github.com/go-numerics/integrate@v0.1.0
data.documentation#Documentation: Design — algorithms, sources, where and why the code departs from them, what is not provided. Verification — how the results were checked against SciPy, mpmath and the netlib Fortran; the full tables are the quadrature table and the ODE table. Performance — timings against SciPy and how they were taken.

The markers are the solver's own // accepted steps, sol.T: no interpolation. func lotka() *plot.Figure { f := func(t float64, y, dydt []float64) { dydt[0] = 1.5*y[0] - y[0]*y[1] dydt[1] = -3*y[1] + y[0]*y[1] } sol, err := integrate.SolveIVP(f, [2]float64{0, 15}, []float64{10, 5}, nil) if err != nil { panic(err) } prey := make([]float64, len(sol.T)) predators := make([]float64, len(sol.T)) for k, y := range sol.Y { prey[k], predators[k] = y[0], y[1] } fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1, plot.FigSize(6.4, 4)) ax := axs[0][0] ax.Plot(sol.T, prey, plot.Marker("o"), plot.MarkerSize(3), plot.Label("prey")) ax.Plot(sol.T, predators, plot.Marker("s"), plot.MarkerSize(3), plot.Label("predators")) ax.SetTitle(fmt.Sprintf("SolveIVP, RK45: %d steps, %d evaluations", sol.NSteps, sol.NFev)) ax.SetXLabel(`time $t$`) ax.Legend() return fig } package main import ( "fmt" "github.com/go-numerics/integrate" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("vanderpol", vanderpol) } // The README's stiff example: van der Pol with mu = 1000 over [0, 3000], // solved with Radau. data.headline-numbers#Headline numbers: Same algorithms, same paths. QUADPACK is ported from the netlib Fortran; the ODE methods follow SciPy’s implementations step for step. Against SciPy 1.18.1, 116 of 124 fixture integrals take exactly SciPy’s subdivision path (same evaluation count, value to 1e-12), and 110 of 120 solve_ivp runs of the ported methods take exactly SciPy’s steps (same nfev, steps, njev, nlu). The remaining differences are explained in Verification: roundoff-limited paths that depend on the last bit, and three integrals where SciPy’s C translation of QUADPACK departs from the Fortran and this port agrees with the Fortran. Faster. 6–8× SciPy on quad (3× without counting Python callbacks), 90–190× on solve_ivp (RK45, DOP853, Radau, BDF; same step sequences), 8–16× on odeint/LSODA (Performance). Verified. Fixtures from SciPy and mpmath, the netlib Fortran as a second oracle, a negative control on the coefficients, 100 % statement coverage with -race, CI lanes on amd64, arm64, riscv64, loong64, ppc64le, s390x, 386 and arm.
data.not-provided#Not provided: Complex-valued integrands and states, vectorized right-hand sides, sparse or banded Jacobians, quad_vec, cubature, tanhsinh, solve_bvp and the legacy ode class. LSODA is an automatic Runge–Kutta/BDF switch, not a port of ODEPACK’s Adams/BDF LSODA: same purpose, different evaluation counts (see design.md).

data: integrate provides what scipy.integrate provides for quadrature and initial value problems, in pure Go, with the same algorithms, defaults and diagnostics. Where an algorithm is a port, it follows its reference line by line, so that a run here and a run of the reference on the same problem take the same steps; verification.md measures how far that holds.
data.bdf-orders-15#BDF (orders 1–5): Shampine & Reichelt, “The MATLAB ODE Suite”, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 18 (1997) — the NDF variant (κ = −0.185, −1/9, −0.0823, −0.0415) — with the quasi-constant step size implementation of SciPy’s bdf.py: a table of backward differences rescaled by change_D whenever the step changes, order selection after order+1 equal steps, at most 4 Newton iterations.
data.common-machinery#Common machinery:
SolveIVP is SciPy’s solve_ivp loop: one accepted step at a time, events located on the step’s dense output with Brent’s method (SciPy’s brentq, xtol = rtol = 4·eps), TEval filled from the dense output, terminal events counted per event. The initial step is Hairer–Nørsett–Wanner’s (Solving ODEs I, II.4) as select_initial_step computes it; error norms are RMS norms of the error scaled by atol + rtol·|y|; finite-difference Jacobians are SciPy’s num_jac (per-column step factors adapted from call to call, a retry for columns lost in roundoff). Evaluations made for those Jacobians are reported separately (NFevJac), because SciPy does not count them in nfev.
Step-size factors use Python’s built-in max/min semantics, which matter when an estimate is NaN: max(0.2, nan) is 0.2, so a step is rejected and shrunk where math.Max would propagate the NaN. A NaN step size ends the integration with ErrStepTooSmall (SciPy loops forever there, for instance on y₀ = 0 with atol = 0, where every error scale is zero).
data.explicit-rungekutta-rk45-rk23-dop853#Exp: RK45: Dormand & Prince, J. Comput. Appl. Math. 6 (1980); free 4th-order interpolant of Shampine, Math. Comp. 46 (1986). RK23: Bogacki & Shampine, Appl. Math. Lett. 2 (1989), with its cubic Hermite interpolant. DOP853: Hairer’s dop853.f (Hairer, Nørsett & Wanner, Solving ODEs I, II.10): 12 stages, the 5th/3rd-order blended error estimate, the 7th-order dense output with 3 extra stages (evaluated only when a dense output is needed, as SciPy does). The tableaux are SciPy’s (rk.py, dop853_coefficients.py), which are the published ones; dop853_coefficients.go is generated from them. Step-size control is SciPy’s: safety 0.9, factors in [0.2, 10], no increase right after a rejection.
data.fixed-rules#Fixed rules: FixedQuad is the n-point Gauss–Legendre rule (nodes by Newton’s method on the three-term recurrence from Tricomi’s initial guesses, cached per n); Romberg is the removed scipy.integrate.romberg (Richardson extrapolation of the trapezoid rule, DivMax levels); Romb, Trapezoid, CumulativeTrapezoid and Simpson are the sample rules, Simpson with Cartwright’s correction for an even number of samples as SciPy ≥ 1.11. The *ND variants apply them along an axis of an ndarray.Array.
data.interfaces#Interfaces: Functions are Go funcs: func(x float64) float64 for integrands, func(t float64, y, dydt []float64) for right-hand sides (the derivative is written, not returned, so steps allocate nothing), and func(t float64, y []float64, jac []float64) for row-major Jacobians. Results are plain slices; Solution.YArray, ODESolution.EvalArray and Odeint return *ndarray.Array in SciPy’s layouts (sol.y is n × len(t), odeint is len(t) × n). Not provided: complex-valued integrands and states, vectorized right-hand sides, sparse Jacobians and jac_sparsity, banded Jacobians and the ml/mu/ixpr/mxordn/mxords/hmin/tcrit options of odeint, quad_vec, cubature, tanhsinh, solve_bvp, and the legacy ode class.
data.lsoda-style-switching-lsoda-odeint#LSODA:
ODEPACK’s LSODA (Petzold, SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput. 4 (1983)) pairs Adams methods with BDF and switches by comparing the step sizes each would take. This package does not port it. Its LSODA pairs the explicit Dormand–Prince methods (RK45, or DOP853 when the smallest rtol is below 1e-6) with the BDF above:
non-stiff → stiff: Hairer’s stiffness detector (Solving ODEs II, IV.2; the test inside dopri5/dop853): after each accepted step hλ ≈ |h|·‖f(y₁) − f(ỹ)‖ / ‖y₁ − ỹ‖ (ỹ the argument of the last internal stage, also at t + h) estimates |h| times the dominant eigenvalue; when it exceeds the stability boundary (3.25 for RK45, 6.1 for DOP853) on 15 steps without 6 consecutive steps below, the step is limited by stability, not accuracy, and BDF takes over with the current step size; stiff → non-stiff: every 5 BDF steps the spectral radius ρ of the Jacobian BDF holds is estimated by power iteration; when |h|·ρ < 1 on two consecutive checks, the explicit method would be stable at BDF’s step size and takes over. This keeps the property that matters to an odeint user — a stiff problem is not integrated with a stability-limited explicit method, a non-stiff one not with BDF — but its counts differ from ODEPACK’s: on the stiff fixtures it uses 1.2–2.2× the right-hand-side evaluations of ODEPACK (Jacobian columns included on both sides). Odeint reports the method of the last step in MUsed (1 explicit, 2 BDF) with ODEPACK’s meaning.
data.multiple-integrals#Multiple integrals: NQuad nests Quad calls exactly as SciPy’s nquad does (variable 0 innermost, ranges of a variable may depend on the outer ones, per-level options); DblQuad and TplQuad are its two- and three-dimensional forms with SciPy’s argument order (f(y, x), f(z, y, x)). AbsErr is the largest one-dimensional error estimate, as in SciPy; NEval counts integrand calls.
data.quadpack-quad#QUADPACK (Quad):
Source: R. Piessens, E. de Doncker-Kapenga, C. W. Überhuber, D. K. Kahaner, QUADPACK, A Subroutine Package for Automatic Integration, Springer 1983; the double-precision Fortran at netlib.org/quadpack.
Go Fortran used for qagsCore + qk21 dqagse, dqk21 finite range, no weight qagsCore + qk15i dqagie, dqk15i [a, ∞), (-∞, b], (-∞, ∞) via x = a + (1-t)/t qagpe dqagpe break points (Points) qawoe, qc25f, fourierMoments dqawoe, dqc25f cos(ωx), sin(ωx) on a finite range qawfe dqawfe Fourier integrals on [a, ∞) qawce, qc25c dqawce, dqc25c Cauchy principal value of f(x)/(x-c) qawse, qc25s, qmomo dqawse, dqc25s, dqmomo (x-a)^α (b-x)^β · {1, log(x-a), log(b-x), both} qelg, qpsrt, qcheb, qk15w, gtsl dqelg, dqpsrt, dqcheb, dqk15w, LINPACK dgtsl epsilon algorithm, error ordering, Chebyshev coefficients, weighted 15-point rule, tridiagonal solve The translation keeps the Fortran’s 1-based arrays, constants (d1mach values), loop bounds and the order in which subintervals are bisected and extrapolated; the goto structure becomes for/break/continue with the labels named in comments. QuadResult carries QUADPACK’s result, abserr, neval and last; ier becomes a *QuadError wrapping one sentinel per code (1 ErrLimit, 2 ErrRoundoff, 3 ErrBadIntegrand, 4 ErrExtrapolation, 5 ErrDivergent, 6 ErrInvalidInput, 7 ErrCycles). For codes other than 6 the estimate is still returned, as SciPy returns it with an IntegrationWarning.
The dispatch is SciPy’s quad: limits are swapped (and the result negated) when b < a, the routine is chosen from the limits and the weight, break points are de-duplicated and restricted to the open interval, a cos/sin weight on (-∞, b] integrates f(-x) on [-b, ∞). SciPy’s wvar is split into typed fields (Omega, Alpha/Beta, C). EpsAbs/EpsRel default to 1.49e-8; a negative value switches a criterion off (SciPy’s epsabs=0).
Deliberate departures from the netlib text, all three in code paths where the Fortran is wrong:
dqc25s accumulates res24 = res12 + cheb24(i)*rg(i) in one loop of its integr = 2 branch, a known typo; the intended res24 + ... is used. dqawfe with ω = 0 integrates over (0, ∞) instead of (a, ∞); a is used. dqagpe’s point sorting and dqawce’s limit swap are not reproduced because Quad hands both routines ordered input; dgtsl’s singular-matrix exits are dropped (the moment systems are never singular). The Chebyshev moments of QAWO are kept per bisection level as dqc25f keeps them in chebmo/momcom, including the MaxP1 bound and the reuse across QAWF cycles. SciPy 1.18.1’s C translation of QUADPACK mishandles maxp1 smaller than the number of levels and differs from the Fortran on two other fixture integrals; the netlib Fortran, compiled with gfortran, settles each case and this port agrees with it (see verification.md).
data.radau-iia-order-5#Radau IIA (order 5): Hairer & Wanner, Solving ODEs II, IV.8, and radau5.f, as restructured in SciPy’s radau.py: the collocation system is solved by simplified Newton on the transformed variables (one real and one complex LU of μ/h·I - J), at most 6 iterations with the convergence-rate test; the error estimate is radau5’s, refined once after a rejection; the step controller is Gustafsson’s predictive one; the Jacobian is recomputed only when Newton converges slowly. Dense LU with partial pivoting (pivot choice as LAPACK’s getrf, |re|+|im| for the complex matrix) replaces LAPACK.

data.method#Method:
bench/compare.sh runs the Go benchmarks of bench_test.go and the same problems through SciPy (bench/scipy_bench.py, under uv run --with scipy --with numpy) alternately, five rounds, and reports the median of each side. Each SciPy figure is the median of 7 repeats of a timed loop lasting about 0.2 s; each Go figure is go test -bench with -benchtime 1s.
SciPy’s time includes calling the Python integrand or right-hand side, which is the price of writing it in Python, not of SciPy’s algorithms. The script also estimates that part: it counts the calls SciPy makes on one run and multiplies by the cost of one call of the same Python function measured alone. The last column divides SciPy’s time without that part by Go’s: what remains is SciPy’s own machinery (QUADPACK in C for quad, NumPy-level Python for solve_ivp, ODEPACK in Fortran for odeint and method="LSODA").
Host: Apple M4 Max (16 cores), macOS, Go 1.27.2, Python 3.12.12, SciPy 1.18.1, NumPy 2.5.4. The machine is shared with other jobs: uptime gave load averages of 7.4 at the start and 8.2 at the end of the run below (16 cores), so absolute numbers carry some noise; the ratios are stable across rounds.
data.reading-the-numbers#Reading the numbers: quad: SciPy’s QUADPACK is compiled C, and 55–62 % of its time is the Python integrand. The same subdivision (same evaluation count, see verification.md) costs 3× less here without the callbacks, 6–8× with them. solve_ivp: SciPy’s RK45, DOP853, Radau and BDF are written in Python on NumPy; per step they pay NumPy call overhead on 2-element arrays, which the callbacks do not explain (they are 2–14 % of the time). The step sequences are the same as here, so the 80–190× is per-step overhead, not a different amount of work. LSODA and odeint: SciPy runs ODEPACK’s Fortran; most of odeint’s time on Robertson is the Python right-hand side. ODEPACK’s own work is about 2× ours on that problem. The comparison is between two different algorithms (see design.md): on Van der Pol μ = 1000 this package’s switching method uses 2 337 evaluations to ODEPACK’s 1 803, on Robertson 2 175 to 1 683, and is still faster in wall time because each evaluation is a Go call. Allocation: a Quad call allocates its subinterval workspace (6 allocations for QAGS); an ODE step allocates only what it stores in the Solution (the state at each output time) plus, for Radau, the interpolant reused as the next step’s predictor. To reproduce: ROUNDS=5 ./bench/compare.sh (needs uv on the PATH).

data: Everything here is reproduced by go test ./...; the tables are regenerated with INTEGRATE_REPORT=1 go test -run VerificationReport ..
data.coverage#Coverage: 100 % of statements, with -race, on arm64 and amd64 (the CI gate runs on Linux, macOS and Windows). The quadrature branches that only adversarial integrands reach are driven by the branch-search fixtures above, checked against SciPy like the others; the few branches unreachable from the public API (qelg with fewer than three entries, the tails of dqagse/dqawfe) have direct unit tests.

data.odes-153-runs-against-solve_ivp#ODEs: 15:
ode-table.md lists every run: exponential decay, harmonic oscillator, Lotka–Volterra, Van der Pol μ = 1, Brusselator, the Arenstorf orbit (all six methods, rtol 1e-3, 1e-6, 1e-9), and the stiff Van der Pol μ = 1000, Robertson, HIRES and OREGO (Radau, BDF, LSODA; with and without an analytic Jacobian where one is given). Errors are scaled by atol + rtol·|y_ref|, so 1 means “at the requested tolerance” (global errors exceed local tolerances on long or chaotic runs, for SciPy as for us).
Same step sequence: for the ported methods (RK45, RK23, DOP853, Radau, BDF), nfev, the number of steps, njev and nlu are all identical to SciPy’s on 110 of 120 runs on arm64 (109 on amd64). The step times agree to 1e-12 to 1e-8 relative (the error estimates are differences of nearly equal numbers, so the summation order of the stage combinations shows up in the last digits of h). The 10 other runs (Radau and BDF on harmonic 1e-9, Arenstorf 1e-6, VdP μ = 1000, OREGO) differ by 0.04–1.1 % in nfev, where one borderline step decision tipped the other way; their accuracy is the same as SciPy’s (0.0104 vs 0.0112, 47.5 vs 56.9, … see the table). Accuracy: every ported run is as accurate as SciPy’s at the same tolerances (identical runs give identical end states). Events: a falling ball (terminal impact, direction −1, plus an apex event) with all six methods: event times agree with SciPy to 1e-12 and with the exact 2.025769006530… s, and nfev equals SciPy’s for the five ported methods; a counting terminal event (terminal = 3) stops at the third zero of cos t, as SciPy. t_eval, dense output, backwards integration agree with SciPy to 1e-9 (RK45 defaults) and 1e-12 (DOP853, rtol 1e-8). data.quadrature-124-integrals-against-scipys-:
quad-table.md lists them all: smooth integrands, end-point singularities (x^-0.9, log x/√x), oscillatory and infinite ranges, break points, the four algebraic-logarithmic weights, Cauchy principal values, Fourier integrals, divergent integrals, and configurations found by a branch search over integrand families that drive every diagnostic of every driver (roundoff, interval too small, extrapolation failure, divergence, limits, QAWF cycle failures).
Same subdivision path: the number of integrand evaluations equals SciPy’s on 116 of 124 integrals on arm64 (115 on amd64), and the values agree to 1e-12 relative wherever the path is the same. Accuracy: on every integral with a reference and no diagnostic, the true error is below the returned error estimate. The 8 differences: qawo_div (∫ cos(30x)/x, divergent) and br_qawo_small (∫ cos(x)/|x−0.3|): SciPy 1.18.1 stops early (1355 and 2505 evaluations); the netlib Fortran takes 6035 and 2685 evaluations with values 140.956644439315767 and 67.6282900830324536, which this port reproduces exactly (TestNetlibOracle). qawo_maxp1 (∫₀¹ cos(200x)/√x with maxp1=2): same counts, but SciPy returns 0.0806726 with ier = 0, while the Fortran and this port return 0.0842501986376902, which mpmath confirms to 3e-16. SciPy’s C translation mishandles a moment table smaller than the number of bisection levels. qawc_tiny, br_x_m12_rel, br_x_m12_abs, br_pts_x_m12_50, br_qawo_div, br_qawf_ier4: tolerances at the roundoff limit or divergent integrals, where the path is decided by the last bit of f and of each rule. Perturbing |x|^-1.2 by one ulp moves SciPy itself from 777 to 945 or 735 evaluations; the Fortran, SciPy and this port each take their own path (the Fortran gives 3105 evaluations on qawc_tiny, SciPy 3075, this port 3375). All report the same diagnostic and values within the error estimates. Go’s math.Pow and the fused multiply-adds Go emits on arm64 are the bit-level differences. Multiple integrals (dblquad, tplquad, nquad on rectangles, a triangle and a simplex) agree with SciPy to 1e-13; fixed rules (trapezoid, simpson with odd/even and uneven samples, cumulative_trapezoid, romb, fixed_quad, roots_legendre) to 1e-14.

data: This package is an independent Go implementation of the parts of scipy.optimize that scientific notebooks use most. A census of 339 notebooks set the order: minimize, minimize_scalar, scalar roots, root/fsolve, least_squares/curve_fit, linprog, brute, check_grad and approx_fprime. SciPy, MINPACK and L-BFGS-B are cited below only as references and as test oracles.
data.api-conventions#API conventions: Callbacks take the point first and write their outputs into the slices that follow: Func(x), Grad(x, g), FuncGrad(x, g), Hess(x, h), Jac(x, J). Matrices are row-major []float64. ndarray: *ndarray.Array appears where arrays are natural (curve-fit data, sigma, LP constraint matrices), and results have …Array() accessors. Options are structs whose zero values select SciPy’s defaults. Errors: invalid input returns an error wrapping ErrInput, ErrDimension, ErrBounds or ErrMethod. Non-convergence is reported in Success/Status/Message, as SciPy reports it, not as an error.
data.brute-checkgrad-approxfprime#Brute, Chec: Brute evaluates numpy.mgrid’s grid with the same point formula, takes the first minimum as argmin does (NaN counts as the minimum), and polishes it with Nelder–Mead, as fmin does. Workers evaluates the grid in parallel. CheckGrad and ApproxFprime are check_grad and approx_fprime, with SciPy’s default absolute step of 1.49e-8.
data.curvefit--curvefitmodel#CurveFit / Curve:
scipy.optimize.curve_fit:
Method: LM through Leastsq without bounds, TRF through LeastSquares with bounds. sigma: a 1-D array divides the residuals; a 2-D covariance whitens them with its Cholesky factor (go-ndarray linalg.Cholesky, then forward substitution). Covariance: With LM it is cov_x. With TRF it is the pseudo-inverse of JᵀJ from the SVD of J. Singular values below eps·max(m,n)·s₀ are discarded. For a tall J the SVD is taken of R, since JᵀJ = RᵀR. It is scaled by the reduced χ² unless AbsoluteSigma is set. It is +Inf (CovOK false) when it cannot be estimated. Errors: non-convergence returns ErrNotConverged together with the partial result, where SciPy raises RuntimeError. Parallelism: Workers evaluates the model over the samples in parallel, from 2048 samples up. The result is bit-identical to the serial run.
data.fidelity-policy#Fidelity policy:
Each routine is a port of a published algorithm. Wherever SciPy’s implementation of that algorithm is itself a reference, the port follows it statement by statement, so that on the same problem it takes the same iterates. The test suite replays SciPy 1.18.1 on fixtures that testdata/gen/*.py generates. It checks solutions, objective values, status codes and messages. It also compares iteration and evaluation counts; where counts are not asserted equal, they are logged side by side.
Three things make floating-point agreement possible, or explain where it stops:
No fused multiply-add. Python never fuses a*b + c. Go fuses it on arm64, ppc64le, s390x, riscv64 and loong64, which changes the last bit and, over many iterations, the path. Every product that feeds an addition in the ported code is wrapped in float64(). The Go specification makes that conversion a rounding point that forbids fusion. The wrapping was applied mechanically by a small go/ast rewriter. As a result, every algorithm gives bit-identical iterates on amd64 and arm64. The oracle must not fuse either. SciPy’s macOS arm64 wheel is built with Apple clang’s default -ffp-contract=on, and its compiled kernels (MINPACK, L-BFGS-B, the C root finders) contain fused instructions. The MINPACK fixtures were therefore generated with the x86_64 wheel under Rosetta, which has no FMA. The L-BFGS-B port was checked against SciPy’s own lbfgsb.c, compiled without contraction and linked to a sequential BLAS: per-iteration f values agree bit for bit on 11 problems, including 513 iterations of Rosenbrock n=100. Against the wheel itself, Accelerate’s blocked BLAS kernels round differently. With an analytic gradient this only shows on long runs: Rosenbrock n=100 takes 513 iterations here and 514 in SciPy. libm. Go’s math.Exp, math.Cos and math.Pow can differ from the platform C library in the last ulp. On test functions built from + − × ÷ and sqrt only, the paths are identical, and the tests assert that. On functions calling exp, sin, cos or pow, a last-ulp difference can move an iterate across a decision. There the tests assert accuracy only.
data.leastsq-and-leastsquareslm-minpack-lmdif:
The Levenberg–Marquardt method with Moré’s (1978) trust region, ported from the same C MINPACK: lmpar, qrsolv, qrfac, fdjac2.
Leastsq mirrors scipy.optimize.leastsq. cov_x is computed as SciPy does: R is inverted in the style of LAPACK dtrti2, the rows are permuted, and the result is invR·invRᵀ. LeastSquares with method LM follows least_squares' call_minpack: It always calls lmder, using approx_derivative for a missing Jacobian. The default budget is max_nfev = 100·n. x_scale='jac' maps to MINPACK’s mode 1; an explicit scale gives diag = 1/x_scale. Statuses are mapped to least_squares’ codes.
data.leastsquarestrf#LeastSquares(TRF):
The trust-region reflective method of Branch, Coleman & Li (1999), ported from SciPy’s _lsq/trf.py and _lsq/common.py (dense, tr_solver='exact'):
Bounds: Coleman–Li scaling, and iterates kept strictly feasible. Step choice: the best of three candidates: the trust-region step clipped at the first bound and stepped back by θ, its reflection off that bound, and the constrained Cauchy step. Subproblem: solved exactly from a thin SVD, with Moré’s safeguarded Newton iteration for the Levenberg–Marquardt parameter. Loss and scaling: the robust losses (soft_l1, huber, cauchy, arctan) rescale J and f as SciPy does, and x_scale='jac' scaling never decreases. Counting: Nfev excludes finite-difference evaluations, as in least_squares. SVD: it comes from go-ndarray’s linalg.SVD, the Golub–Kahan/QR algorithm of LAPACK gesvd. A faster one-sided Jacobi SVD was measured and rejected: on exactly rank-deficient Jacobians it returns exact zeros where LAPACK returns tiny values, and SciPy’s path depends on those tiny values. Tall matrices (m ≥ 1000 and m ≥ 11n/6, the regime where LAPACK’s gesdd also factors QR first): the Jacobian is reduced by Householder QR and only the n×n R is decomposed. Uᵀf is obtained as U_Rᵀ(Qᵀf), with no m×n U ever formed. The fixtures, all smaller than 1000 rows, take the direct path.
data.linprog#Linprog:
HiGHS, SciPy’s default, is out of reach. Two dense solvers are provided instead, with documented limits.
Revised simplex (default): Two phases with bounded variables. Phase one starts from slack and artificial variables; phase two fixes the artificials at zero, so any left in the basis stand for redundant rows. Dantzig pricing, switching to Bland’s rule after 50 degenerate pivots. Harris’s two-pass ratio test with bound flips. Dense LU with product-form updates, refactorised every 64 updates. Interior point: the homogeneous self-dual method of Andersen & Andersen (2000) with Mehrotra predictor–corrector, ported from SciPy’s legacy _linprog_ip.py with its standard form and settings. The normal equations are solved by Cholesky, then LU, then least squares, in that fallback order. Presolve: after SciPy’s _presolve: it removes empty rows and columns and fixed variables, and detects linearly dependent equality rows. Duals: they follow HiGHS’s sign convention. Final check: SciPy’s _check_result downgrades a status that is inconsistent with the returned point. Not done: singleton-row presolve, crossover, scaling, warm start, sparse matrices.
data.minimize#Minimize:
Method Algorithm Reference followed NelderMead Nelder & Mead (1965) simplex; adaptive coefficients of Gao & Han (2012); bounds by reflection of the initial simplex and clipping SciPy _minimize_neldermead (stable ordering, maxfev unwinding exactly where SciPy raises) Powell Powell (1964) conjugate directions with the Press et al. replacement test; Brent line searches, bounded line searches restricted to the box, arctan mapping for half-infinite ranges SciPy _minimize_powell, _linesearch_powell, _line_for_search CG Polak–Ribière with Powell’s β ≥ 0 (PR+), strong-Wolfe search plus the sufficient-descent condition on the next direction (Nocedal & Wright §5.2) SciPy _minimize_cg BFGS Inverse-Hessian BFGS (Nocedal & Wright Alg. 6.1), strong-Wolfe line search SciPy _minimize_bfgs; deviation: the update is applied in O(n²) as a rank-two correction instead of two dense n×n products (O(n³)). It is the same formula in exact arithmetic but rounds differently. It is the main reason BFGS is 10–20× faster at n=100. NewtonCG Truncated Newton (Nocedal & Wright Alg. 7.1): CG on the Newton system with forcing term min(0.5, √‖g‖₁), stopped on negative curvature SciPy _minimize_newtoncg, including its three Hessian sources and the order of the two gradient calls in its finite-difference Hessian-vector product, which decides how often the cache hits LBFGSB L-BFGS-B 3.0 (Byrd, Lu, Nocedal & Zhu 1995; Zhu et al. 1997; Morales & Nocedal 2011): generalized Cauchy point with a breakpoint heap, compact limited-memory matrices, subspace minimisation with the 3.0 projection and backtrack, Moré–Thuente line search SciPy 1.18.1’s C translation lbfgsb.c, one subroutine per method (cauchy, hpsolb, bmv, formt, formk, cmprlb, subsm, lnsrlb, matupd, LINPACK dpofa/dtrsl) Iterate parity is asserted on the problems built from arithmetic only (Rosenbrock n=2, Beale, Himmelblau): 36 of the 38 runs there take SciPy’s exact path. The two exceptions:
BFGS with finite differences on Rosenbrock, because of the O(n²) update above. Newton-CG on Beale, which differs by one gradient call (52 against 53) with the same iterations and function evaluations. Shared machinery:
Line searches (dcsrch.go, linesearch.go). The Moré–Thuente search (MINPACK-2 dcsrch/dcstep, as in SciPy’s _dcsrch.py) is used by BFGS, CG, Newton-CG and L-BFGS-B. Its fallback is the Nocedal–Wright bracketing/zoom search (SciPy’s scalar_search_wolfe2, _zoom, _cubicmin, _quadmin). Evaluation counting (scalarFunc). It reproduces SciPy’s ScalarFunction. There is a one-point cache, so f and ∇f are each computed and counted at most once per x. A finite-difference gradient reuses the cached f(x) and adds its evaluations to Nfev, and every gradient counts once in Njev. Finite differences (numdiff.go). This is SciPy’s approx_derivative: 2-point and 3-point schemes, relative or absolute steps with the same defaults (√eps·max(1,|x|), or SciPy’s absolute 1.49e-8 for BFGS/CG and 1e-8 for L-BFGS-B), and steps adjusted to stay inside bounds, going one-sided when needed. Wrapper semantics. These come from scipy.optimize.minimize: the tol mapping to each method’s tolerance, clipping x0 into the bounds, removing variables fixed by equal bounds for L-BFGS-B with finite differences, and status 99 when the callback stops the run.
data.minimizescalar-bracket-fminbound#Minimiz: These are Brent’s (1973) parabolic/golden method, the golden-section search, the bounded variant of Forsythe, Malcolm & Moler’s FMIN (fminbound), and the downhill bracket search. All four are ported from SciPy’s Python implementations (Brent, _minimize_scalar_golden, _minimize_scalar_bounded, bracket), messages included. A failed bracket search returns the best of its three points, as SciPy’s _recover_from_bracket_error does. On arithmetic-only test functions the iterates are identical to SciPy’s. One subtlety: SciPy computes the golden constant 1 − 0.61803399 at run time in float64, while a Go constant expression would be exact and round differently.
data.root--fsolve-minpack-hybrdhybrj#Root / F:
Powell’s hybrid method, ported from SciPy 1.18.1’s C translation of MINPACK (Moré, Garbow & Hillstrom 1980):
Kernels: dogleg, qrfac with column pivoting, qform, r1updt, r1mpyq, and the forward-difference fdjac1. Layout: storage is column-major, as in MINPACK, so every sum keeps the reference order. Norm: MINPACK’s three-accumulator enorm is kept, because a different norm alone breaks bit parity. Defaults: as SciPy’s _root_hybr: maxfev 200(n+1) without a Jacobian and 100(n+1) with one, factor 100, xtol 1.49012e-8. Messages are SciPy’s. Deviation: Nfev excludes the two extra calls SciPy’s Python wrappers make (a shape check and an initial evaluation). SciPy’s reported nfev is always ours + 2. Not ported: band and col_deriv.
data.scalar-roots#Scalar roots: Brentq, Brenth, Ridder, Bisect follow SciPy’s C implementations (scipy/optimize/Zeros/*.c, by Charles Harris, BSD licence): Brent with inverse quadratic or hyperbolic extrapolation (Bus & Dekker 1975), Ridders (1979) with SciPy 1.18’s underflow-safe update, and bisection. Defaults are xtol 2e-12, rtol 4·eps and 100 iterations. C’s MIN macro returns b when a is NaN, unlike math.Min. Ridder relies on this after an infinite midpoint value, so it is reproduced (cmin). A NaN function value stops the search with an error, as SciPy raises. Through RootScalar it becomes a result instead, as SciPy’s root_scalar does. Newton covers Newton–Raphson, Halley and the secant method, ported from SciPy’s newton (scalar path). RootScalar selects the method by SciPy’s rules.
data.slsqp-constrained-minimisation#SLSQP (co:
Minimize(…, SLSQP, …) is Dieter Kraft’s sequential least-squares quadratic programming method (DFVLR-FB 88-28, 1988), as rewritten in C by SciPy. Sources opened for the port, all BSD-3-Clause or BSD-style:
SciPy v1.18.1 scipy/optimize/src/slsqp.c (__slsqp_body, lsq, lsei, lsi, ldp, ldl_update) and src/nnls.c (Lawson–Hanson NNLS), followed statement by statement, including the reverse-communication state machine (modes 0/1/−1), the augmented problem for inconsistent linearisations (weight 100, ×10 up to five times), the five BFGS resets and the relaxed test with tol = 10·acc; SciPy v1.18.1 _slsqp_py.py, _slsqpmodule.c, _minimize.py and _constraints.py for the driver: evaluation order and counting, clipping the line-search point into the bounds, the removal of fixed variables, the all-fixed shortcut and new_constraint_to_old for NonlinearConstraint and LinearConstraint; Reference-LAPACK v3.12.1 dlarfg, dlarfgp, dlartgp, dlapy2, dgerq2, dormr2 (and the reference BLAS loop orders) for the dense kernels. Kraft’s 1988 report itself was not available to us; the method is cited through SciPy’s code, which references its §2.2.3.
Deviations. dgelsy (least squares with only equality constraints) is replaced by Householder QR with column pivoting and the rank test |R(k,k)| > √ε·|R(0,0)|; SLSQP only reads the rank. Three LAPACK branches that cannot be reached here are omitted and documented in the code. Where SciPy’s NNLS would index out of range on an empty passive set, the loop stops. The go-simd/floats kernels are not used: they reduce in a lane-blocked FMA order that would change the path both against SciPy and between architectures, on vectors of a few dozen entries.
Constraint types. Options.Constraints takes Constraint (SciPy’s dictionary form), NonlinearConstraint (lb ≤ f(x) ≤ ub) and LinearConstraint (lb ≤ A·x ≤ ub). All three reduce to equality and inequality blocks, the form later constrained methods will share. Unlike SciPy, which warns, other methods return ErrMethod when constraints are given.
Fidelity. Fixtures come from SciPy’s x86_64 wheel run in a linux/amd64 container (tools/slsqporacle --platform linux/amd64), because SciPy’s macOS arm64 wheel contracts a*b + c into fused multiply-adds. On 100 runs (36 Hock–Schittkowski problems and 10 stress cases, each with and without derivatives, plus option and new-style-constraint variants): every status agrees, 88 take SciPy’s exact path (identical nit, nfev, njev, with x to 1e-7 and f to 1e-9 relative), and 96 reach the same objective to 1e-6. On each of the 12 others SciPy’s own arm64 and x86_64 wheels also disagree with each other, so the path is decided by last-bit rounding (HS13 is degenerate; HS23, HS29, HS38 run near-singular updates; Infeasible, SingularEq, SingularEq3 hinge on a pivot that is zero in exact arithmetic). Go results are bit-identical on amd64 and arm64. slsqporacle diff a.json b.json lists the cases on which two fixtures disagree, which is how the wheels were compared; the harness and tools/slsqpbench have their own tests, run in CI, which need neither Python, Docker nor a quiet machine (v0.3.1).
data.trust-constr-interior-point#trust-constr:
Minimize(…, TrustConstr, …) is SciPy’s trust-constr: the Byrd–Omojokun trust-region SQP method for equality-constrained problems (Lalee, Nocedal and Plantenga 1998), and, as soon as there is an inequality or a bound, the barrier (interior-point) method of Byrd, Hribar and Nocedal (1999) around it. Sources opened for the port, BSD-3-Clause:
SciPy v1.18.1 scipy/optimize/_trustregion_constr/: minimize_trustregion_constr.py (driver, state, stop tests, statuses 0–4, bounds widened by one ulp), tr_interior_point.py (barrier subproblem, slack scaling, τ = 0.995, μ and tolerance ×0.2, trust radius ×5), equality_constrained_sqp.py (normal and tangential steps, merit penalty, second-order correction, radius updates), qp_subproblem.py (modified_dogleg, projected_cg, box and sphere intersections), projections.py (null-space, least-squares and row-space operators by QR with column pivoting, SVD when the Jacobian is singular), canonical_constraint.py (eq/less/greater/interval classification); SciPy v1.18.1 _hessian_update_strategy.py (BFGS, skip_update, init_scale='auto') and _differentiable_functions.py (ScalarFunction and VectorFunction): when gradients and BFGS updates happen — at every new point, rejected trial points included, and again for a constraint when its multipliers change — which is what makes the evaluation counts comparable; SciPy v1.18.1 _constraints.py and _minimize.py (dictionary constraints become NonlinearConstraint(fun, 0, 0 or inf) with a BFGS Hessian each; no clipping of x0; tol sets gtol, xtol and barrier_tol); Reference-LAPACK v3.12.1 dlaqp2 (pivoted QR with norm downdating). The two papers themselves were not available to us; they are cited through SciPy’s code.
Kernels. The projections, CG and BFGS products use go-simd/floats (Dot, Axpy, Xpby, Scale). That is allowed here because SciPy’s own iterates depend on its BLAS and on SuperLU (bounds-only problems use the sparse augmented system), so bit-identity is out of reach anyway; it means trust-constr’s results are not bit-identical across architectures, unlike SLSQP’s. The projections always use dense QR with column pivoting.
Fidelity. tools/slsqporacle --method trust-constr --platform linux/amd64 replays the 100 SLSQP runs with trust-constr. Success or failure agrees with SciPy on all 100 (two raise in both: more equalities than variables, an ErrInput here), the status itself on 93 on arm64 and 94 on amd64 (the others are gtol against xtol, both successes), and every successful objective is within 1e-5 of SciPy’s or 1e-4 of the known optimum. 65 runs take SciPy’s exact path on arm64 and 69 on amd64. SciPy’s own arm64 and x86_64 wheels disagree with each other on 35 runs (slsqporacle diff), almost all with finite-difference derivatives; counts are asserted on every other run except four listed in trustconstr_fixture_test.go (HS48/fd, Rosen-free/fd and the rank-deficient SingularEq3 with and without derivatives), on amd64 and arm64.
Why four runs differ from SciPy. slsqporacle trace --platform linux/amd64 records every objective, gradient and constraint evaluation and every iteration of one SciPy run, plus the arguments and results of modified_dogleg and projected_cg (monkey-patched in the interpreter fed on standard input); go test -run TestTraceDump records the same events for this package (OPTIMIZE_TRACE_CASE, OPTIMIZE_TRACE_OUT); slsqporacle tracediff finds, tag by tag, the first event that differs bitwise and the first beyond a tolerance. Of the five runs left in v0.4.0:
HS21/jac and HS35/jac were our defects. SciPy’s projected_cg computes rt_g = norm(g)**2 and the tangential radius sqrt(r**2 - norm(dn)**2): the square of the rounded norm, which is not the dot product g·g; and its boundary step is x + theta*alpha*p, that is x + (theta*alpha)*p, where the port applied theta to the already scaled alpha*p. Both now follow the source (sqNorm, and theta*alpha in projectedCG), and both runs take SciPy’s exact path (60 and 46 iterations; the same change makes the nit of HS48/fd equal to SciPy’s). A/B: with the unchanged go-simd/floats kernels this alone fixes both. HS48/fd and Rosen-free/fd are last-bit rounding. The first divergence is a tangential step 1e-16 to 5e-16 away (relative), in a run whose projections cannot be the cause (Rosen-free has no constraint, so Z = I): only dot products and updates of two to five entries remain. go-simd/floats fuses each multiply-add (Axpy is math.FMA; its Dot accumulates in fused lanes), while NumPy rounds y + alpha*x in two operations and the OpenBLAS core that produced the fixture — OPENBLAS_VERBOSE=2 prints Core: Nehalem, because Docker on Apple silicon emulates a CPU without AVX or FMA — sums ddot left to right below 16 entries (kernel/x86_64/ddot.c). On real x86_64 hardware OpenBLAS picks the Haswell or SkylakeX core, which fuses, and SciPy’s arm64 wheel fuses too: there is no single SciPy to match to the bit. The finite-difference Jacobian then turns 1e-16 into 4e-8 (HS48) or 1e-7 (Rosen-free) one or two iterations later, and the run stops one gradient earlier or later; the iteration count is SciPy’s (asserted). An experiment with unfused, sequential kernels below 16 entries (no go-simd) gave 66 and 67 exact runs in two variants against 65, and made Rosen-free/fd exact in the first, but moved other runs off the path (HS35/jac in the second): rounding the kernels differently trades runs rather than removing the cause, so the kernels were not changed. SingularEq3/jac and /fd are the SVD. The Jacobian is rank-deficient, so the projections use scipy.linalg.svd (LAPACK dgesdd) and here go-ndarray’s SVD: the first Newton point differs by 1.5e-16 and a trial point is evaluated once more at iteration 3. The iteration count is SciPy’s (asserted). On these four the status, solution and objective are asserted as on every other run, and the iteration count must equal SciPy’s.
Omitted. keep_feasible (strict bounds), sparse Jacobians and the NormalEquation/AugmentedSystem projections, the SR1 strategy and user-supplied constraint Hessians, verbose reports. Branches of SciPy’s code that cannot be reached with these options (an infinite trust radius, the infeasible-iteration counter of projected CG) are documented in the code.

data.what-the-numbers-say#What the numbers sa: Small problems (n = 2): SciPy’s time is almost all fixed Python overhead (argument handling, ScalarFunction wrappers, NumPy calls on 2-element arrays) plus about 10 µs per callback. Go spends nanoseconds on each. The gap is 100–450× and stays above 85× even after crediting SciPy with free callbacks. BFGS at n = 100: in this run our update was O(n²) where SciPy does two dense n×n matrix products per iteration. That gave the 5× left once SciPy’s callbacks are removed. A bit-exact update replaced it for a while and was slower than SciPy; since v0.8.0 the O(n²) update is the default again (see the current timings above). L-BFGS-B at n = 100: SciPy’s core is compiled C with BLAS, and ours is Go. With callbacks counted we are 3.7× faster. Without them the cores are within 2× of each other, ours ahead. Finite differences: each forward-difference gradient costs n Python calls in SciPy and n inlined Go calls here. At n = 100 that is 73×. curve_fit with 10⁴ points: SciPy was faster in the table above. SciPy’s model call is one vectorised NumPy expression per evaluation, so it pays no per-point Python overhead. Its MINPACK and LAPACK kernels are compiled C. These two rows were measured before the MINPACK kernel work of optimize PR #7, after which the 2026-10-17 run gave 1.07× (LM) and 1.27× (TRF); they have not been re-timed since, because the host’s load has stayed above refbench’s limit of 8. Both sides take the same path: same data (SHA-256), same p0 and tolerances, the same forward-difference Jacobian and the same counts (21 evaluations for LM, 6 for TRF). A profile (2026-11-09) puts 65% of LM and 54% of TRF in the model sweeps: CurveFit calls a Go closure once per point (about 3.2 ns per point with math.Exp), where SciPy calls its NumPy expression once per sweep. Model.Vec (v0.7.0) takes the model over arrays, called once per sweep, so it can use go-simd/floats’ vector Exp (about 1.35 ns per element). With the same arithmetic per point it gives the fit of the per-point model to the last bit; with the vector Exp (0.511 ULP) the fit agrees with SciPy within the fixture tolerance and takes the same evaluations. Timed on 2026-11-09: 1.59× (LM) and 1.74× (TRF) SciPy’s speed, against 1.06× and 1.24× with the model per point. brentq: 32×, almost entirely because the 8 callbacks are Go calls.

Special mathematical functions in pure Go (no cgo, no assembly): the gamma family, error functions, incomplete gamma and beta functions and their inverses, Bessel functions, zeta functions, combinatorics, logistic helpers and complete elliptic integrals — with an element-wise layer over go-ndarray.
🌐 Website · 📚 Documentation
It is the numerical foundation of the go-numerics statistics library: every distribution’s cdf and quantile function is computed with these functions, so their accuracy is the product. Each function is measured in ULPs against mpmath at high precision, over its whole domain — tails, zeros, poles, huge and tiny arguments, subnormals, NaN and ±Inf — and SciPy is measured on exactly the same points.

data.complex-functions#Complex functions:
github.com/go-numerics/special/cmplx (new in v0.4.0) is a drop-in superset of the standard library’s math/cmplx. Changing the import path is enough: the names and signatures are the same, with C11 Annex G special values.
New functions: Mul and Div (the Annex G product and quotient), Proj, Log2, Log1p and Expm1. Unchanged from math/cmplx: Abs, Phase, Conj, Polar, Rect, Inf, NaN, IsInf and IsNaN are one call to a correctly specified real function, and are re-exported as they are. Rewritten: every other function. The algorithms are FreeBSD msun’s (as NumPy’s npymath carries them), carried in double-double where float64 loses accuracy. Underlying real functions: sin, cos and tan use this package’s Payne–Hanek reduction, and atan2 is table-driven double-double. import "github.com/go-numerics/special/cmplx" cmplx.Tanh(400 + 1i) // (1+0i); math/cmplx: NaN cmplx.Log(1 + 1e-10i) // (5e-21+1e-10i); math/cmplx: real part 0 cmplx.Pow(1i, 2) // (-1+0i), exactly; math/cmplx: (-1+1.2e-16i) Each part is measured in ulps against mpmath at 192 and 320 bits. The fixtures cover the tiny, subnormal, huge and near-overflow regions, the branch points, and both sides of every branch cut. Worst part per function:

Two budgets sit above the target, and both are open issues:
Asinh, Asin, Acos and Acosh: 3 ulp (#26). Pow, region unit: 4500 ulp (#27), inside the design’s (2 + |y log x|) ulp bound. Every region is listed in docs/accuracy-complex.md, and the design is docs/design-complex.md. Timing against NumPy’s complex ufuncs has not been measured yet.
data.double-double-arithmetic#Double-double a: github.com/go-numerics/special/dd (public since v0.3.0) is the double-double type the functions above are built on: dd.DD{Hi, Lo} with Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Sqrt, Exp, Log, the exact accumulators Dot, DotDD, Sum, AddProd (every product exact, accumulation in double-double, so an ill-conditioned dot product keeps about 100 bits), and conversions FromInt64, FromBig, Parse (a decimal string to the nearest double-double), (DD).Big, (DD).Float. Relative errors, fuzzed against math/big: Add 3u², Mul 5u², Div 15u²+56u³ (u = 2⁻⁵³); Sqrt is measured (under 8u²). It is the arithmetic behind double-double QR with iterative refinement (the NIST StRD Filip and Wampler problems to 15 digits). ExpMant and ExpReductionMargin expose the exponential’s argument reduction, for callers that must know whether two nearby arguments take the same table entry (go-statistics/stats uses it; it is the single copy of this package).
data.functions#Functions:
Each row gives the Go function and, in brackets, the scipy.special function it is measured against — the pairing comes from the harness (bench/perf_test.go and testdata/gen/fam_*.py), not from transliterating a name, which is why Log1pExp is scipy’s softplus and LogGamma is gammaln. 64 of the 67 carry such a pairing; — marks the three that do not, and the notes under the table say what they are. readme_scipy_test.go reads the harness and fails if this column drifts from it.

Kn — scipy does have kn; this package simply does not measure it against it. The bracketed name is scipy’s, not a measurement. In — scipy has no in, and cannot: it is a Python keyword. Iv at integer order is the equivalent, and In(n, x) is Iv(float64(n), x). Kn/Kv and Jn/Jv stand in the same relation, which is why Jn is bracketed jv: scipy’s jn is a deprecated alias of jv. LogGammaSign — no scipy counterpart in any spelling; scipy splits the two results across gammaln and gammasgn. The 20 …To slice kernels — GammaTo, ErfTo, XlogyTo and the rest — are the batch form of the function they are named after and compute the same thing, so they share its scipy equivalent rather than earning rows here. One exception is worth knowing: TrigammaTo is exported while Trigamma is not, so that kernel has no scalar form in the public API. It is psi’(x), which scipy spells polygamma(1, x) — the same function Polygamma already provides.
Zeta and HurwitzZeta share one scipy name, zeta(x, q=None), which takes the second argument optionally. LogFactorial is bracketed as a call rather than a name because the function is gammaln with its argument shifted, which is what the harness measures it against.

data.portability#Portability:
Pure Go; CI runs the full accuracy suite on amd64, arm64, 386, arm (32-bit), riscv64, loong64, ppc64le and s390x, compiles the tests for every go tool dist list target, and holds a 100% statement-coverage gate.
One finding along the way: on amd64, Go’s math.Log (assembly) returns about -709.09 for every subnormal argument (it should go down to -744.44); this package never calls it on a value that can be subnormal.

Accuracy has a price. Measured against SciPy 1.18.1 on one core (refbench, tag v0.6.0, 2026-11-10, 10 000-point calls, host load 4.8–7.9, valid run; ratios are Go time over SciPy time):

Accuracy is what this package sells, so it is measured, published and enforced by the test suite, not asserted.
The per-region table is generated: accuracy-table.md. This page explains how it is produced, which algorithm each function uses and where it comes from, what the negative control showed, and where the package is not (yet) as good as it should be.
data.algorithms-and-sources#Algorithms and so:
Two building blocks run through everything:
Double-double arithmetic (github.com/go-numerics/special/dd, a public package since v0.3.0; fuzzed against math/big with the error bounds of the double-word algorithms: Add 3u², Mul 5u², Div 15u²+56u³, u = 2⁻⁵³): error-free transformations (Knuth’s TwoSum, Dekker’s Fast2Sum, FMA-based TwoProd) and the double-word algorithms of Joldes, Muller & Popescu (ACM TOMS 44(2), 2017). dd.Exp and dd.Log are table-driven after Tang (ACM TOMS 15(2), 1989 and 16(4), 1990), carried to double-double (about 2^-76 and 2^-72 relative), with 300-bit mpmath tables. Float64 kernels (kernels.go): table-driven exp and log after Tang in the arrangement of ARM’s optimized-routines (exact Cody–Waite / TwoProd reductions, 400-bit tables from go -C tools run ./genkernel) returning an unevaluated hi + lo — exp to about 2^-68 relative, log to 2^-68 absolute — at a few floating-point operations; the elementary families below use them instead of dd on their main paths, which remains for the tails and for the incomplete gamma/beta functions. Fitted polynomials (testdata/gen/fit.py and, for the tables added with the float64 kernels, the Go port go -C tools run ./genfit; zz_*_coeffs.go): Chebyshev interpolants of a well-chosen regular part of a function, fitted to mpmath at 200 bits on short pieces, degree chosen so that the interpolation error is below 2^-64, constant term kept in double-double. The function’s zeros, poles and logarithmic singularities are factored out analytically, so the fitted part is smooth and the relative accuracy holds where the function vanishes. function algorithm source Gamma Γ(1+t) = 1 + t(t-1)F(t) on [-1/2, 1] with F fitted; exact-factor recurrence (x - k is exact), the product carried as hi + lo for 1 <= x < 10 and in double-double for 0 < x < 1 and -34 < x < 0 (there and in the reflection region, a float64 evaluation with a proven error bound returns the double-double path’s float64 bit for bit whenever the bound decides the rounding: gamma-fastpath.md); Stirling’s series (DLMF 5.11.1) above 10, (x-1/2)log x - x + S(x) formed from the log kernel with every leading sum exact and S as hi + lo (about 2^-63 absolute), then the exp kernel; reflection with sin(πx) reduced exactly below -34; integers from a correctly rounded factorial table DLMF 5.5, 5.11; core fitted to mpmath LogGamma, LogGammaSign, GammaSign log1p of Γ(1+t)-1 near the zeros at 1 and 2; the same Stirling expression above 10; exact factors for -34 < x < 0; reflection below DLMF 5.11.1, 5.5.3 Digamma ψ(1+t) = (t - r)D(t) with the positive zero r in double-double and D fitted (the form of Boost.Math’s digamma_imp_1_2); recurrence with double-double reciprocals; on [2, 10) ψ fitted directly (constant and linear terms exact); asymptotic series above 10 (DLMF 5.11.2) with log x from the log kernel; for -40 < x < 0, exact-factor recurrence, redone with a 2^-100 evaluation when the terms cancel (near the negative zeros); reflection with cot(πx) in double-double below DLMF 5.5, 5.11; Boost.Math digamma.hpp Polygamma (-1)^(n+1) n! ζ(n+1, x); for n = 1, ψ’(x) directly: the asymptotic series from 10 with its two leading terms as hi + lo, the recurrence below with every 1/(x+k)² as hi + lo DLMF 25.11.12, 5.15.8 Beta, LogBeta below 10, Γ(a)Γ(b)/Γ(a+b) from the double-double core with the rounding of a+b corrected to first order; above, log Γ(b) - log Γ(a+b) as one cancellation-free Stirling expression (-a log b - b log1pmx(a/b) - (a-1/2) log1p(a/b) + S(b) - S(a+b)) added to log Γ(a), or for 10 <= a <= b <= 64a the three Stirling log-gammas combined directly (bounded cancellation); the series of log1p(x) - x below x = 1/64 and S(b) - S(a+b) with the differences of powers factored; float64 kernels throughout DLMF 5.11.1, 5.12.1 Erf, Erfc, Erfcx x E(x²) for |x| <= 1/2; erfcx fitted on [1/2, 8] and as x·erfcx(x) in 1/x² beyond (the Gaussian factor removed, as in Cody 1969); exp(-x²) from x² carried exactly (exp kernel), multiplied in before the single rounding; the pieces evaluated with their constant and linear terms exact Cody, Math. Comp. 23 (1969); DLMF 7.12 Ndtr, LogNdtr erfc of -x/√2 carried in double-double (the rounding of x/√2 is what costs SciPy up to 1e12 ulp in the lower tail); log Φ as log erfcx(z) - z² - log 2 in the lower tail, with log erfcx fitted directly (and as log(z erfcx z) in 1/z² beyond 8), and log1p(-Φ(-x)) in the upper DLMF 7.2, 7.12 ErfInv, ErfcInv, Ndtri evaluated directly, no iteration: erfinv(p) = p R(p²) for |p| <= 1/2 and erfcinv(q) = X(√(-log q)) on 20 pieces down to the smallest subnormal q, both fitted to mpmath; 1 + g(s)2^-s with g = (ζ(s)-1)2^s fitted on (6, 64); reflection with sin(πs/2) reduced exactly below -1 (trivial zeros exact) DLMF 25.4.1 HurwitzZeta Euler–Maclaurin summation (the arrangement of Cephes zeta.c) with q+k exact in double-double, powers through double-double log/exp and terms summed with a common exponent (no intermediate overflow); the number of direct terms chosen so 15 Bernoulli terms reach 2^-64; for 1 < s <= 64 the float64 kernels with 25 Bernoulli terms and the shorter shift w >= 7.3 + s/2 (bound computed with mpmath, checked by a test) DLMF 25.11.5; m < -1 by the imaginary-modulus transformation DLMF 19.7.5, 19.12; A&S 17.3.34–36 GammaP, GammaQ, GammaPInv, GammaQInv method selection of DiDonato & Morris as in Boost.Math’s gamma_incomplete_imp and Cephes igam: power series (terms in light double-double pairs while above 2^-16 of the sum), Legendre’s continued fraction (depth from the Wallis recurrences, value summed backwards as P/Q, top level in double-double), Temme’s uniform expansion for a > 20 near x = a (its sum generated straight-line, testdata/gen/fitgo), small-a upper-tail series; the complement formed from the double-double tail; the prefactor x^a e^-x/Γ(a) formed as a double-double logarithm (a·log1pmx((x-a)/a) and Stirling, no cancellation for any a) and exponentiated once. Inverses: DiDonato–Morris starting value (Boost find_inverse_gamma), then a bracketed Halley iteration in log x on log of the smaller tail against its exact target (one float64 evaluation of the tail per step, g = log1p((T-t)/t) near the root) DiDonato & Morris, ACM TOMS 12(4) 1986; DLMF 8.7, 8.9, 8.11, 8.12; Boost.Math gamma.hpp, igamma_inverse.hpp (BSL-1.0); Cephes igam.h BetaInc, BetaIncC, BetaIncInv, BetaIncCInv TOMS 708 (BRATIO with BPSER, BUP, BFRAC, BGRAT, BASYM, APSER, FPSER) ported from SciPy’s cdflib.c, with every power prefix x^a y^b/B(a,b) formed as a double-double logarithm, BASYM’s λ = (a+b)y - b in double-double; BPSER in Euler’s all-positive form (DLMF 8.17.8), shared with BUP, in light double-double pairs; BFRAC’s fraction summed backwards from the depth its forward pass finds, the top level from the closed forms in double-double. data.headline#Headline:
Over 62 fixtures (419 regions, about 250 000 points), the maximum error of this package is at or below SciPy’s in 418 of 419 regions; the one exception is k1 at small x, 1.05 ulp against SciPy’s 1.05 (both use Boost’s K1 rational; ours is larger in the third digit).
About half an ulp (correctly rounded or nearly) for the gamma family, erf/erfc/erfcx and their inverses, Ndtr/Ndtri/LogNdtr, zeta and Hurwitz zeta, polygamma, combinatorics, logistic helpers and elliptic integrals — including the tails, the zeros of log Γ at 1 and 2, the poles, the trivial zeros of ζ and the subnormal range, where SciPy’s errors run from tens of ulps to 1e15 ulp or a wrong NaN/Inf. Incomplete gamma and its inverses: at most 2.1 ulp (SciPy: up to 8.9e15). Incomplete beta: at most 9 ulp; its inverses at most 20 ulp for parameters >= 1e-3 (SciPy: up to 4.5e15). Bessel functions: at most about 5 ulp everywhere, 0.5 ulp at the zeros of J0, J1, Y0, Y1 (SciPy: 1e10–1e12 ulp there) and under 2 ulp for arguments up to 1e300 (SciPy loses every digit). Not solved: the beta inverses with a or b far below 1e-3, where the root depends on digits beyond double-double (both this package and SciPy can return a wrong root; the budget is +Inf and documented). Bold in accuracy-table.md marks a region where ours is at or below SciPy; where both are “wrong” the row is bold too.
data.how-the-error-is-measured#How the error:
Oracle. Every fixture value is computed by mpmath 1.4.1 twice, at 192 and at 320 bits of working precision (with extra precision where the formula cancels, e.g. log Γ(a) + log Γ(b) - log Γ(a+b) for huge arguments, which is evaluated with 1200 extra bits). A point whose two evaluations differ by more than 2^-80 relative is dropped, and the drop is counted in the fixture header: an oracle that silently lost precision must not become the truth the tests are held to. (The first runs dropped 247 logbeta points this way, which led to the extra-precision fix.)
Exact reference, not a rounded one. Each row stores the mpmath value as a double-double hi + lo, hi being the correctly rounded float64. The error of a result y is |y - (hi + lo)| / ulp(hi), so a correctly rounded result scores at most 0.5, and the half-ulp of the reference’s own rounding is not added to anyone’s error.
SciPy on the same points. The generator also stores SciPy 1.18.1’s result for the same float64 arguments, and the Go test measures it exactly as it measures this package. SciPy is a point of comparison, never the reference.
Regions. Each function’s domain is cut into regions — tails, the neighbourhood of zeros and poles, huge and tiny arguments, subnormals, special values (NaN, ±Inf, ±0) — sampled with a fixed seed (log-uniform where the scale matters). About 1000 points per region; 160 000 points over all fixtures. A result that should be NaN or ±Inf and is not (or the reverse) is reported as wrong.
Budgets. TestAccuracy fails if any region’s maximum error exceeds its budget (budgets_test.go: 1.5 times the error measured when the budgets were generated, at least 1 ulp). The suite runs on amd64, arm64, 386, arm, riscv64, loong64, ppc64le and s390x in CI.
Same bits on every architecture. Go may fuse x*y + z into one multiply-add, and does on arm64, ppc64le, s390x, riscv64 and loong64 but not on amd64, 386 or arm; package math’s Exp, Log, Pow, Sin, … also differ by architecture (assembly versions, or pure Go compiled with fusion). Every product here is therefore rounded explicitly (float64(a*b)) or fused on purpose with math.FMA — tools/fmalint checks the source, and its --objdump mode checks the arm64 binaries — and those math functions come from internal/libm, Go’s pure-Go implementations with the same treatment. TestArchHash compares the output bits of every public function on a fixed grid with testdata/archhash.golden in every CI lane.

data.known-limitations#Known limitations: Speed. Double-double costs a factor of about 3 single-threaded for most functions and 10–15 for the Bessel functions of real order, Hurwitz zeta and the incomplete beta function (perf.md). Digamma at its negative zeros: 31 ulp at 1e-16 relative distance from a zero (SciPy: 2.5e17); limited by double-double itself. LogBeta where log B(a, b) ≈ 0 (a, b near 1): 30 ulp; the three log-gammas carry ~2^-56 relative errors that the cancellation exposes (SciPy: 45 000). Bessel: Jn/Yn within 5.4 ulp at the zeros of orders >= 2; Jv at negative non-integer order and x < |v| 7.2 ulp, Ive at negative order 12 ulp (both from the reflection formula’s cancellation); K1/K1e at small x tie with SciPy (1.05/1.49 ulp, Boost’s rational unchanged); orders above 1e7 only where the series or the large-x expansion applies (NaN elsewhere); J and Y at x = +Inf return the limit 0 where SciPy returns NaN. Incomplete beta: up to 5 ulp for a, b in [1, 100) and 9 ulp for a, b in [100, 1e4) near the mean in this table (SciPy: 447 and 3487); BetaIncCInv 20 ulp for a, b in [1e-3, 1) (51 on amd64; SciPy 4.5e15). These are the fixtures’ measurements before the backward BFRAC and the positive BPSER series; a dense re-check (2000 points per region) gives 1.05 and 3.1 ulp and 1.2 ulp for those three; the table has not been regenerated. Beta inverses with a or b far below 1e-3: I_x(a, b) is flat to beyond 2^-100 over most of (0, 1), so the float64 root depends on digits past double-double; results can be wrong (so are SciPy’s). Budget +Inf, documented at BetaIncInv. Oracle caveat: mpmath’s own betainc returned an identical wrong value at both precisions for b = 1e-200 (the self-check cannot catch an error that does not depend on precision), so the incomplete-beta oracles compute the smaller tail by series or tanh-sinh quadrature instead. Complex arguments are not implemented (the nd layer rejects complex dtypes). Not yet implemented: Struve, Airy, Kelvin, spherical Bessel, incomplete elliptic integrals, Lambert W.

data.where-scipys-result-is-not-a-number-it-s:
Some SciPy “wrong” entries in the table are conventions, not errors; they are listed so the table is not misread:
gammaln(5e-324) and gammaln(-5e-324) return inf (exact: 744.44). erfcinv(5e-324) returns inf (exact: 27.2133). betaln(a, b) returns nan for 528 of the 1000 points with a, b in (100, 1e300] (exact values are finite, e.g. betaln(5.08e223, 7.77e195) = -5.05e197). github.com/go-numerics/special/cmplx (new in v0.4.0) is a drop-in superset of the standard library’s math/cmplx. Changing the import path is enough: the names and signatures are the same, with C11 Annex G special values.
New functions: Mul and Div (the Annex G product and quotient), Proj, Log2, Log1p and Expm1. Unchanged from math/cmplx: Abs, Phase, Conj, Polar, Rect, Inf, NaN, IsInf and IsNaN are one call to a correctly specified real function, and are re-exported as they are. Rewritten: every other function. The algorithms are FreeBSD msun’s (as NumPy’s npymath carries them), carried in double-double where float64 loses accuracy. Underlying real functions: sin, cos and tan use the package’s Payne–Hanek reduction, and atan2 is table-driven double-double. go get github.com/go-numerics/special@v0.4.0 import "github.com/go-numerics/special/cmplx" cmplx.Tanh(400 + 1i) // (1+0i); math/cmplx: NaN cmplx.Log(1 + 1e-10i) // (5e-21+1e-10i); math/cmplx: real part 0 cmplx.Pow(1i, 2) // (-1+0i), exactly; math/cmplx: (-1+1.2e-16i)

data.what-mathcmplx-gets-wrong-and-why#What m:
math/cmplx evaluates each textbook formula directly. That fails in the finite range in three ways:
Overflow of intermediates: cosh(2x) in Tanh, e^x in Exp. Cancellation near the unit circle and the branch points: log(hypot), and log(iz + sqrt(1-z²)) in the inverse functions. The real functions underneath: math.Sincos and math.Tan keep the reduced argument to an absolute accuracy, so they lose up to hundreds of ulps near their zeros and poles. math.Atan2(-5e-324, -1e130) returns +π.

data.method#Method: One core on both sides. refbench sets GOMAXPROCS=1 around the run and starts the SciPy worker with OMP/OPENBLAS/MKL/VECLIB_*_THREADS=1. The nd/ rows therefore run on one goroutine; the earlier multi-core column is gone. Like with like: one call over an array on both sides. Every row times one call over the same 10 000 points. The SciPy body is one ufunc call (result array allocated by the call, as the Go side allocates its own); the ufunc’s per-call overhead (about 1 µs) is amortised over the points. Three Go bodies are timed against the same SciPy call: the scalar function in a loop over the points (Gamma), the public array kernel (GammaTo: the Go counterpart of a ufunc loop, no call per element), and the nd wrapper (nd/Gamma, kernel plus allocation and dtype handling). A scalar loop calls the function once per element through a function value; SciPy’s ufunc loop does the same through a C function pointer, so that row is fair, and the kernel rows are the strict array-against-array comparison. data.what-was-done-33#What was done (#33): BetaIncInv/BetaIncCInv allocate nothing (#36); nd.Map2/Map3 run one direct loop for same-shape and scalar operands, bit-identical to the old path (#37). Gamma on 0 < x < 1 and x < 0 runs a float64 evaluation with an a-priori error bound and falls back to the double-double path only when the bound cannot decide the rounding, so the results are bit-identical (derivation and fallback rates: gamma-fastpath.md); sinPi/cosPi reduce their argument with an exact a - 2⌊a/2⌋ instead of math.Mod. v0.5.6: I1, I1e, K1, K1e from fitted octave interpolants (results change, more accurate); Comb by an exact integer recurrence, Factorial2 from a table, Factorial (n >= 10) and Xlog1py through certified float64 kernels, GammaSign without math.Mod (bit-identical). Not done: float64 fast paths for the remaining double-double functions. A fast path is acceptable only if a certified error bound decides when float64 is already correctly rounded, so that the bits do not move; none has been derived for the open gaps above.
